title: Lullaby of the Dawn
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Elva is a kannagi, a warrior priest chosen by the divine to fight creatures from the black sea; his cursed, black-stained limbs mean all kannagi die young, and villagers fear him until the boy Alto moves in and vows to free him (Tokyopop blurb; Anime UK News). Eight years later Alto's presence seems to heal the curse, and his glimpse inside the secretive Monastery that trains kannagi makes him doubt what he has been told (Anime UK News). An ongoing Boys' Love fantasy, rated OT 16+.
life_message: Devoted love can heal what fate and institutions say is unchangeable.

content.note: Nightly monster fights (review; no gore described); MU Blood and Gore, Murders in later volumes (to verify).
Curse and early death; dark ambience (review; MU).
Adult male romance; no sexual scenes in vol. 1 (review). MU lists sexual scenes and a sexual-assault backstory in later volumes; database only, capped (to verify).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Elva's worth affirmed by Alto despite village fear (blurb).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Alto moves in uninvited and defies the Monastery's limits (review).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Personal bond outweighs village and institution (review).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Divine calling and folklore frame the world, though questioned (review).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival against the sea balanced by love (blurb).

folkways.japan: The term kannagi draws on Japanese words for shrine mediums, and the island setting echoes Japanese shrine and sea-folk traditions.

delivery.evidence: Reviewer praises slow, info-dump-free worldbuilding and does not cast clear villains (Anime UK News).
delivery.note: Doubt about the Monastery arises through the mystery rather than argument; its later portrayal is not in the sources.

winners_losers: Alto and Elva's bond gets the story's sympathy; the Monastery's secrecy is put under suspicion (review).
to_verify: Possibly understated: MU lists sexual scenes, sexual assault and child abuse in later volumes; only vol. 1 was reviewed.
